questions.prompt: In the cache-aside pattern, what happens on a cache miss?

options.text: The request fails and returns an error
The app loads from the database, stores it in Redis with a TTL, and returns it
Redis loads it from the database automatically
The value is written to the database only

questions.explanation: Cache-aside is application-managed: on a miss the app fetches from the source, populates Redis (usually with a TTL), and returns the value.

questions.prompt: What is the key risk of the write-behind (write-back) pattern?

options.text: Writes are extremely slow
Data buffered in the cache can be lost if Redis crashes before flushing to the database
Reads always miss
It cannot use TTLs

questions.explanation: Write-behind acknowledges writes at the cache and flushes to the database asynchronously, so a crash before the flush loses those buffered writes.

questions.prompt: Which techniques help prevent a cache stampede? Select all that apply.

options.text: Adding random jitter to TTLs so keys don't all expire at once
A recompute lock so only one request rebuilds a missed key
Refreshing hot keys early, before they expire
Removing all TTLs so keys never expire

questions.explanation: Jitter, a recompute lock, and early refresh all reduce stampedes. Removing TTLs entirely causes permanent staleness and doesn't solve the herd — it's not a fix.

questions.prompt: Why keep a TTL on cache entries even if you invalidate them on writes?

options.text: TTLs make writes faster
If an invalidation is ever missed, the stale entry still expires on its own — mistakes self-heal
Redis requires a TTL on every key
TTLs prevent cache hits

questions.explanation: A TTL is a safety net: even if a delete/update-on-write is lost, the entry eventually expires, so staleness can't persist indefinitely.

questions.prompt: The pattern where the application checks the cache and, on a miss, loads from the database and populates the cache is called cache-______. (one word)
questions.explanation: Cache-aside (also called lazy loading) is the most common caching pattern, managed by the application.

questions.prompt: What does server-assisted client-side caching (CLIENT TRACKING) provide?

options.text: It disables the Redis cache entirely
Clients cache keys locally, and Redis sends invalidation messages when those keys change
It forces all reads to go to the database
It makes Pub/Sub durable

questions.explanation: With CLIENT TRACKING, clients keep local copies of fetched keys and Redis notifies them to invalidate a copy when the key changes — near-zero-latency reads that stay reasonably fresh.
